title: Errands
goal: Run everyday errands — bank and ATM, pharmacy, mobile shop, tailor, barber, laundry and courier — and say what you need to get done and by when.
intro:
Life in Karachi or Lahore runs on errands: a top-up from the corner mobile shop, a new SIM with your **شناختی کارڈ**, a shirt from the **درزی** before Eid, a trim at the **نائی**. In almost all of them you are getting **someone else** to do something for you, and Urdu has a special verb form for exactly that: the **causative**, made with **-وا-** (کروانا, بنوانا, سلوانا).

This unit teaches the causative, how to say what you need done (**مجھے بال کٹوانے ہیں** 'I need a haircut'), and how to ask when it will be ready (**کب تک ہو جائے گا؟**). Shopkeepers are spoken to with **آپ** and the polite -یں forms (**کر دیں، دے دیں**), usually softened with **بھائی** — while your friend standing next to you gets **تم** and **یار**.

grammar.title: Getting it done: causative verbs with -وا-
grammar.body:
When you **get someone else** to do a job, Urdu uses a causative verb, made by adding **-وا-** to the stem:

**کرنا** do → **کروانا** get done
**بنانا** make → **بنوانا** get made
**بدلنا** change → **بدلوانا** get changed
**کاٹنا** cut → **کٹوانا** get cut
**نکالنا** take out → **نکلوانا** get taken out
**دھونا** wash → **دھلوانا** get washed
**سینا** sew → **سلوانا** get stitched

A long vowel in the stem usually shortens (کاٹ → کٹ, نکال → نکل) and stems ending in a vowel add ل (دھو → دھل, سی → سل), so learn each causative as a word. You will also hear shorter forms without و, especially **کرانا** for کروانا — same meaning.

**Who does the job** takes **سے**: میں نے درزی **سے** قمیض سلوائی 'I had the tailor stitch my shirt'. Usually you just leave the person out: بال کٹوانے ہیں 'I need a haircut'.

Causatives are transitive, so in the past they take **نے** and agree with the thing, not with you: میں نے بال **کٹوائے** (بال m. pl.), امی نے قمیض **سلوائی** (قمیض f.).

Add **لینا** when the job is done for your own benefit — very common in speech: میں نے بال **کٹوا لیے** 'I got my hair cut'.

**The trap:** the plain verb means you did it yourself. میں نے بال کاٹے means you took the scissors to your own head! At the barber, tailor or repair shop, always reach for the -وا- form.

grammar.title: Saying what you need done: مجھے … کروانا ہے
grammar.body:
You met **مجھے جانا ہے** 'I have to go' in unit 15. The same pattern is how you announce your errand: **مجھے + thing + infinitive + ہے**.

When the thing is named, the infinitive **agrees with it**, just like an adjective, and ہے becomes ہیں for plurals:

مجھے فون ٹھیک **کروانا ہے** (فون m.)
مجھے قمیض **سلوانی ہے** (قمیض f.)
مجھے پیسے **نکلوانے ہیں** (پیسے m. pl.)
مجھے بال **کٹوانے ہیں** (بال m. pl.)

You will sometimes hear the plain -نا form with feminine and plural things (مجھے قمیض سلوانا ہے), but the agreeing form is standard and sounds better.

At the counter people usually drop مجھے: **بال کٹوانے ہیں** 'a haircut, please', **یہ پارسل بھیجنا ہے** 'I'd like to send this parcel'. For 'will I have to…?' use **ہوگا**: کیا مجھے فارم بھرنا **ہوگا**؟

examples.en: I need to get my phone fixed.
I need to get a shirt stitched.

examples.roman: bāl kaṭvāne haiṃ, kitnā intizār hai?
examples.en: I'd like a haircut — how long's the wait?

grammar.title: Will it be ready? ہو جائے گا، مل جائے گا
grammar.body:
At the counter you usually care **when the job will be done**, not who does it. For this Urdu uses the intransitive 'it happens' verb plus **جانا**:

**ٹھیک ہو جانا** to get fixed
**بن جانا** to get made, be ready
**مل جانا** to be available, to get (lit. be found)
**دھل جانا** to get washed · **سل جانا** to get stitched · **بدل جانا** to get changed

کب تک ٹھیک **ہو جائے گا**؟ 'When will it be fixed by?' — شام تک **بن جائے گا** 'It'll be ready by this evening.' — یہ دوا **مل جائے گی**؟ 'Do you have this medicine?'

The verb agrees with the thing: فون ٹھیک ہو جائے **گا**, سم مل جائے **گی**, کپڑے دھل **جائیں گے**.

**تک** means 'by' (a deadline): **کل تک** 'by tomorrow', **پانچ بجے تک** 'by five'. In the habitual it means 'is available': یہ ہر جگہ **مل جاتا ہے** 'you can get it everywhere'.

The shopkeeper's favourite answer is **بس دس منٹ** 'just ten minutes' — plan for half an hour.

culture: Errands in Pakistan are social. You call the man behind the counter **بھائی** or **بھائی جان** and a woman **باجی**; older people are **انکل** and **آنٹی** even if you have never met. You use **آپ** with them and the polite -یں forms (دے دیں، کر دیں), while the friend who came along with you stays **تم** and **یار**. Prices at mobile and repair shops are open to haggling ('ہم پرانے گاہک ہیں' helps), but banks, pharmacies and branded salons have fixed rates. Every neighbourhood has its **درزی**, and before Eid they are booked solid, so take your fabric in at least two or three weeks early — and know that 'کل پکا' (definitely tomorrow) often means a few days. A new SIM needs your **CNIC** (شناختی کارڈ) and a thumbprint check at the franchise. Many people now pay bills and top up through apps such as JazzCash and Easypaisa instead of queueing at the bank. In the diaspora — Bradford, Toronto, Houston, Dubai — the same words carry on: you get a suit **سلوانا** in Lahore and have it couriered over.

tip.title: Do it vs get it done: -وا-
tip.body:
- Add **-وا-** to a verb when **someone else** does the job for you: کرنا → **کروانا**, نکالنا → **نکلوانا**.
- Plain verb = you do it yourself: اے ٹی ایم سے پیسے **نکالے**.
- Causative = you get it done: بینک سے پیسے **نکلوائے**.
- The person who does it takes **سے**: بھائی **سے** بل جمع کروایا.

tip.body:

tip.title: Will it be ready? ہو جائے گا
tip.body:
- To ask when a job will be **done**, use the 'it happens' verb + **جانا**: ٹھیک **ہو جائے گا**, **مل جائے گا**, **بن جائے گا**.
- It agrees with the thing: فون ٹھیک ہو جائے **گا**, سم مل جائے **گی**.
- **تک** = by: شام **تک** 'by this evening'.
tip.pattern: thing + ٹھیک ہو / مل / بن + جائے گا / گی

tip.title: Who does the job: سے
tip.body:
- The person you get to do the job takes **سے**: درزی **سے** کپڑے سلوانے ہیں.
- In the past a causative takes **نے** and agrees with the **thing**: میں نے قمیض **سلوائی** (f.), کپڑے **سلوائے** (pl.).
- The person who actually does it uses the plain verb with نے: درزی **نے** ناپ لیا.
tip.pattern: میں نے + person + سے + thing + causative

lessons.title: At the barber and the parlour

tip.title: For yourself: کٹوا لیے
tip.body:
- Add **لینا** to a causative when it was done for you: میں نے بال **کٹوا لیے** 'I got my hair cut'.
- To the barber, ask with the plain verb — he is the one cutting: تھوڑے سے **کاٹ دیں**.
- Telling others what you're getting done, use the causative: بال **کٹوانے** ہیں.
